summary: We developed HESTIA, a web application that combines active fire hotspot records from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites into an interactive map and burning activity calendar. MODIS has tracked fires at 1 km resolution since 2000, while VIIRS has captured smaller fires at 375 m resolution since 2012. Combining their raw detections causes an artificial spike after 2012, so our pipeline aligns both datasets onto hexagonal H3 grid cells and scales older MODIS records using years when both sensors overlapped. On the dashboard, users can draw custom areas on the map, switch between raw and harmonized layers, click calendar weeks to jump through history, and animate fire spread across daily, weekly, monthly, and multi-year intervals. Reliable multi-decade baselines help forestry teams, researchers, local responders, and communities living with seasonal haze in Southeast Asia spot abnormal fire seasons earlier and separate real environmental changes from differences in satellite hardware.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

HESTIA helps people explore active fire history across Malaysia and nearby regions using NASA satellite detections from MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). Because VIIRS sees smaller fires at 375 m resolution compared to MODIS at 1 km, combining their raw counts creates a misleading jump after 2012. To address this, our backend script groups fire detections onto hexagonal H3 grid cells, compares days when both satellites saw the same fire, and scales older MODIS numbers to match VIIRS. On the web dashboard, anyone can draw a region on the map, switch between raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, or harmonized results, and press play to watch hotspots shift across daily, weekly, monthly, or multi-year intervals alongside a seasonal calendar and trend graph.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We built HESTIA so forestry staff, climate researchers, local responders, and communities affected by seasonal smoke can inspect long-term fire patterns without needing specialized GIS software. Keeping the raw and harmonized views side by side makes it easy to check how our calibration affects the numbers, and statistical anomaly markers (Z > 2) highlight when fire activity genuinely spikes above normal dry-season burning.

Tools, Languages, and Software

Our team developed the data pipeline and backend API in Python using Polars, DuckDB, FastAPI, and H3, and built the frontend in TypeScript and React with Tailwind CSS, Deck.gl, MapLibre, and Apache ECharts. Everything was built on standard personal laptops, packaged with Docker for local testing, and hosted using GitHub and Vercel.

How It Is Creative

The map and charts are linked in both directions. Drawing a custom area on the map immediately updates the burning calendar, historical average, and anomaly spikes for that location, while clicking a cell on the calendar or stepping through the animated timeline moves the active fire view on the map and centers the trend graph around that date.

Factors We Considered

Scanning raw CSV files on every map click felt too slow during early testing, so we pre-grouped observations into compressed Parquet files to keep queries fast in DuckDB. We also accounted for years with an ISO week 53 so the heatmap stays aligned at 52 columns, added fallback scaling factors for areas where MODIS and VIIRS rarely overlap on the same day, and removed unused libraries like pandas and pyarrow so the backend fits within Vercel's 500 MB deployment limit.
